\chapter{In the Kitchen}
\label{ch:ta-in-the-kitchen}
\hlchaptermodality{59}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name curd, ghee, oil, jaggery and sugar in Tamil.}

Complete TA-C59-sugar and say all five words in order.

\section[tayir]{\ta{தயிர்} (tayir) — curd}

\label{lesson:TA-C59-curd}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{kākkai} mean, and what did \emph{paṟavai} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{தயிர்}}
\textbf{\ta{தயிர்}} (\emph{tayir}) — \textquotedblleft{}curd\textquotedblright{}.

Set \ta{பால்}, soured overnight in a covered pot. It is what a Tamil meal finishes on, turned through the last of the \ta{சாதம்}, and it is the thing a hot afternoon is survived with.

The sisters do not agree here at all: Kannada \ka{ಮೊಸರು} (\emph{mosaru}), Telugu \te{పెరుగు} (\emph{perugu}), Tamil \ta{தயிர்}. Three households, three words, one pot.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of five kitchen words.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{tayir}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{tayir}, then \emph{sādam}, and say which one goes on top of the other
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{தயிர்} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}curd\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ney]{\ta{நெய்} (ney) — ghee}

\label{lesson:TA-C59-ghee}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{tayir} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{நெய்}}
\textbf{\ta{நெய்}} (\emph{ney}) — \textquotedblleft{}ghee\textquotedblright{}.

Butter cooked down until the water has gone and only the fat and the smell are left. Short, old, and Tamil's own. Telugu keeps it as \te{నెయ్యి} (\emph{neyyi}); Kannada walked off to \ka{ತುಪ್ಪ} (\emph{tuppa}).

A spoon of it goes over hot \ta{சாதம்} at the start of a meal on a day that matters, which is most of what it does.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ney}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{tayir}, then \emph{ney}, and say which one ends a meal and which one opens it
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{நெய்} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}ghee\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[eṇṇey]{\ta{எண்ணெய்} (eṇṇey) — oil}

\label{lesson:TA-C59-oil}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{ney} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{எண்ணெய்}}
\textbf{\ta{எண்ணெய்}} (\emph{eṇṇey}) — \textquotedblleft{}oil\textquotedblright{}.

The end of it is \ta{நெய்}, standing there unchanged. The front piece is an old name for the sesame seed, so the whole thing began as sesame-fat — and then it widened until it covered every oil a kitchen has, sesame or not.

Kannada kept the same word as \ka{ಎಣ್ಣೆ} (\emph{eṇṇe}); Telugu went to \te{నూనె} (\emph{nūne}). The doubled \ta{ண்} in the middle is the one made with the tongue curled back, held twice as long.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three, and the third is built out of the second.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{eṇṇey}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{ney}, then \emph{eṇṇey}, and hear the first one still sitting inside the second
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{எண்ணெய்} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}oil\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[vellam]{\ta{வெல்லம்} (vellam) — jaggery}

\label{lesson:TA-C59-jaggery}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{eṇṇey} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{வெல்லம்}}
\textbf{\ta{வெல்லம்}} (\emph{vellam}) — \textquotedblleft{}jaggery\textquotedblright{}.

Cane juice boiled down and left alone — no bleaching, no crystals — and sold as a dark heavy lump you break a piece off. Kannada has the same word as \ka{ಬೆಲ್ಲ} (\emph{bella}), with \emph{v} softened to \emph{b}.

In an older Tamil kitchen sweetness meant this before it meant anything white, and \ta{வெல்லம்} still goes into the food that has to taste the way it used to.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{vellam}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{vellam}, then \emph{ney}, and say which of the two a sweet needs
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{வெல்லம்} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}jaggery\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sarkkarai]{\ta{சர்க்கரை} (sarkkarai) — sugar}

\label{lesson:TA-C59-sugar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{vellam} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{சர்க்கரை}}
\textbf{\ta{சர்க்கரை}} (\emph{sarkkarai}) — \textquotedblleft{}sugar\textquotedblright{}.

The refined white kind, beside \ta{வெல்லம்} rather than in place of it. Kannada \ka{ಸಕ್ಕರೆ} (\emph{sakkare}), Telugu \te{చక్కెర} (\emph{cakkera}): one word, lightly redressed three times.

It has travelled further than any other word in this run. Sanskrit \emph{śarkarā} went out through Arabic, Greek and Latin and came back into English as \emph{sugar}, so \ta{சர்க்கரை} and the English word are one word wearing different clothes.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five, and the run is closed: curd, ghee, oil, jaggery, and sugar.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{sarkkarai}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item all five in order — \emph{tayir}, \emph{ney}, \emph{eṇṇey}, \emph{vellam}, \emph{sarkkarai}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{சர்க்கரை} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}sugar\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
